base_properties.human_readable: Digital Money Emergence Boundary (Consumer Holdings Reading)

stakeholders.name: regulatory_bodies_ecb_emi
stakeholders.situation: Define legal categories of money, electronic money institutions (EMIs), and payment services. Enforce the distinction between bank deposits (M1-M3) and directly-held e-money instruments (M4-M5 frameworks). Set capital requirements, licensing standards, and transaction limits. Benefits from boundary-setting authority: each new boundary definition creates regulatory jurisdiction and licensing revenue streams.

stakeholders.name: fintech_issuers
stakeholders.situation: Issue e-money products (digital wallets, stablecoins, prepaid instruments) that consumers can hold directly. Benefit from the consumer-holdings boundary because it legitimizes their products as 'money' rather than 'deposit accounts,' granting regulatory exemptions from full banking capital requirements and opening markets unavailable to non-banks. Can exit by pivoting to asset-management or custodial services if regulatory conditions shift.

stakeholders.name: traditional_banks
stakeholders.situation: Face revenue erosion as deposit-taking transitions from bank accounts to direct consumer holdings of e-money. Obligated to compete with lighter-touch fintech while carrying full capital and reserve requirements that fintech can avoid. Cannot exit without abandoning the deposit base; can only constrain themselves through lobbying for tighter EMI regulation.

stakeholders.name: legacy_payment_networks
stakeholders.situation: See transaction volume and fee revenue migrate from ACH/card networks to direct e-money rails (blockchain, mobile money transfer protocols). The consumer-holdings boundary eliminates the intermediary role of traditional payment operators; transactions settle directly between consumer wallet and recipient without network routing. Can constrain but cannot exit; attempting to compete in e-money issuance triggers regulatory friction.

stakeholders.name: individual_consumers
stakeholders.situation: Gain access to payment instruments held directly in their own custody, reducing reliance on banks for transaction access. Benefit from faster settlement and lower friction. However, lose the implicit deposit insurance and dispute-resolution machinery that banks provide; e-money holdings often lack the regulatory protections of bank accounts. Constrained by limited alternatives and by the fintech issuers' control of wallet terms.

stakeholders.name: unbanked_populations
stakeholders.situation: Are technically enabled by direct consumer holdings to access financial services without bank infrastructure, but lack devices, connectivity, or trust in fintech operators to actualize the benefit. The constraint's definition of 'digital money' centers on consumer agency and direct custody—a premise that presupposes access to identity systems, telecom networks, and regulatory protections unavailable in many global regions.

stakeholders.name: central_banks
stakeholders.situation: Monitor the money supply boundaries and monetary transmission mechanisms as direct consumer e-money holdings grow. Face pressure to redefine M4/M5 categories to maintain control over monetary aggregates and transmission policy. Observe the constraint without direct enforcement authority but with strong structural interest in the boundary definition.

six_questions.coordination_function: Establishes a clear legal and technical category (digital money held directly by consumers) that enables fintech issuers to enter financial services without building bank infrastructure. Coordinates on the boundary definition so that regulatory capital requirements, consumer protections, and transmission mechanisms can be tailored to the properties of e-money (fast settlement, no reserves, programmability) rather than bank deposits.
six_questions.transfer_function: Transfers deposit-taking revenue and payment-transaction fees from traditional banks and payment networks to fintech issuers and regulatory bodies (via licensing and compliance infrastructure). Also transfers settlement risk from network operators to consumer wallet holders (who now bear custody and non-default risk).
six_questions.absent_voices: Unbanked and underbanked populations are structurally excluded—the reading assumes consumer agency, device access, and regulatory legitimacy that these populations lack. Decentralized finance (DeFi) practitioners who claim money exists when code enforces scarcity without regulatory boundary-setting are kept outside the regulatory conversation. Second-order payment intermediaries (remittance services, informal value transfer networks) lose their market position but are not seated in the defining conversation.
six_questions.disappearance_rationale: If direct consumer holdings ceased to be recognized as 'money,' fintech issuers would lose regulatory legitimacy and most would convert to custodial agents (holding money on behalf of customers in bank-regulated accounts). Banks would recover the deposit base. Payment settlement would revert to network-mediated ACH and card rails. The boundary's disappearance would collapse the fintech issuance industry and restore traditional payment intermediaries to bottleneck positions.
six_questions.founding_problem: Pre-1990s, digital value could only circulate through banks (as deposit entries) or payment networks (as authorization to move bank deposits). No consumer could directly hold a cryptographic instrument or digital token outside an institutional intermediary. The founding problem: how to enable direct consumer custody of value in digital form without requiring bank infrastructure or network authorization for each transaction.
six_questions.founding_problem_corroboration: Technical progress (cryptography, mobile networks, distributed ledgers) continues to enable new forms of direct consumer holdings. Regulatory bodies (ECB, FinCEN, FCA) and fintech practitioners attest that the problem remains active: new instruments (stablecoins, central bank digital currencies, tokenized assets) generate novel custody and settlement architectures. Traditional banks and payment networks do NOT attest the problem is live—they frame it as a solved problem (banks already enable digital deposits) or a regulatory hazard (direct holdings lack deposit insurance).

commentary.narrative_context: The consumer-holdings reading of digital-money emergence marks the boundary at the moment when individuals could directly hold and transact with digital instruments outside traditional bank accounts and payment networks. This reading stabilized around 1990s e-purse pilots and formalized with the 2000 EMD (Electronic Money Directive) in the EU, which legally recognized e-money as a category distinct from bank deposits. The reading instantiates a specific normative claim: money exists when it is held and controlled by the individual, not when it is abstracted into an account entry at an intermediary. This reading benefits regulatory bodies (who gain definitional authority and licensing jurisdiction) and fintech issuers (who gain regulatory legitimacy as non-banks). It extracts from traditional banks and payment networks, whose intermediary role becomes optional rather than mandatory. The claim/metric gap is deliberate: extractiveness starts low (18% in 1990 when e-purses were experimental niche products) and rises to 0.62 by 2023 as fintech issuance scaled and captured transaction volume from traditional intermediaries. The constraint is a tangled rope: genuine coordination function (enabling non-bank financial service entry) paired with asymmetric extraction (banks and networks lose revenue and control). The boundary is actively enforced: regulatory bodies issue EMI licenses, set capital requirements, define transaction limits, and prosecute unauthorized money transmission. This reading coexists with two sibling readings of the same kernel—the conceptualization reading (money exists when formalized theoretically, ~1985) and the infrastructure reading (money exists when transferred electronically, ~1972)—each with different beneficiaries, boundaries, and ε values. The three readings are competing frames on when digital money 'really' emerged, held by different communities and producing different policy consequences.
commentary.logic_rationale: Extractiveness rises from 0.18 (1990, experimental niche) to 0.62 (2023, scaled fintech issuance) because the boundary's legitimacy creates a regulatory moat: fintech issuers can offer payments without full banking capital requirements, systematically undercutting banks on fees and speed. Banks cannot exit without losing the deposit base; they are constrained to expensive compliance and risk-based pricing to compete. Theater ratio (0.28) is moderate: regulatory bodies frame EMI oversight as consumer protection (deposit insurance equivalent, KYC/AML enforcement), which is a real function but increasingly performative—the narrative of equivalence stretches thinner as fintech products diverge from bank deposits in structure and risk profile. Suppression requirement (0.41) reflects active enforcement: regulators prosecute unlicensed money transmission, block unauthorized fintech issuance, and maintain technical and legal barriers to entry. The suppression plateaued after 2015 because the boundary had solidified: most would-be fintech entrants were already working within the EMI framework by then. The measurement series are authored on a single shared grid (every metric at every time point: 1990, 2000, 2008, 2015, 2020, 2023) to avoid the temporal misalignment problem documented in OQ-105.
commentary.perspectival_gap: From the regulatory bodies' and fintech issuers' perspective, the constraint solves a real problem—enabling non-bank financial service entry and clarifying legal categories. From the traditional banks' and payment networks' perspectives, the constraint is enforced extraction: they lose mandatory intermediary status and must compete with lighter-touch competitors. From the unbanked populations' perspective (excluded from the conversation), the constraint's definition of 'direct consumer holdings' presupposes device access and regulatory protection they lack. From central banks' perspective, the constraint forces redefinition of monetary aggregates (M4/M5) and complicates monetary transmission mechanisms. The engine will compute different seat-level classifications from these different structural positions: beneficiaries will compute as rope (coordination benefit, low extraction cost); payers will compute as snare or tangled_rope (asymmetric extraction, constrained exit); excluded seats will not appear in the computation.
commentary.directionality_logic: Regulatory bodies hold institutional power, analytical time horizon, and arbitrage-grade exit (they set the rules)—directionality near 0.0 (full beneficiary), effective extraction negative or minimal. Fintech issuers hold organized power, mobile exit (can pivot to custody/brokerage), biographical time horizon—directionality near 0.1-0.2 (modest beneficiary; they collect from margin but depend on regulatory legitimacy). Traditional banks hold powerful status but constrained exit (cannot leave the market without bankruptcy) and face direct extraction—directionality near 0.85-1.0 (full target). Payment networks: same structure as banks, d near 0.85-1.0. Individual consumers: powerless, constrained exit, biographical horizon—beneficiary role (gain access) but also indirect payer (lose deposit insurance protections)—d near 0.5 (symmetric). Unbanked populations: trapped exit, powerless, excluded from conversation—d near 1.0 (full target) but structurally absent from the constraint's operative surface.
commentary.mandatrophy_analysis: The founding problem (enabling direct consumer holdings) remains live but its urgency has shifted. Pre-2008, the problem was urgent: e-commerce and mobile payments were new, and enabling non-bank entry was necessary for innovation. Post-2015, the problem persists but the solution has calcified into a regulatory framework that now blocks certain kinds of innovation (stablecoins, cross-border e-money) while protecting incumbent fintech issuers from new entrants. The constraint is not yet a piton (it still enforces genuine boundaries and distributes real benefits/costs), but it shows signs of mandatrophy—the boundary definition is increasingly disconnected from the technical and economic dynamics that motivated it. The founding problem's status is 'live' because central banks and fintech are still expanding e-money categories (CBDCs, tokenized assets), but the corroboration is weakening: traditional banks dispute that direct consumer holdings are necessary (they offer near-instant digital settlement now) and central banks are moving away from the EMI distinction toward comprehensive digital currency frameworks. The theater ratio's plateauing (staying at 0.28) signals that the constraint's enforcement machinery is becoming maintenance-of-status rather than active value-delivery.
commentary.kernel_context: This constraint is the consumer_holdings_reading of the digital_money_emergence_boundary kernel. The kernel is a contested moment: when did digital money 'really' emerge? This reading instantiates the normative claim that money exists when individuals can hold it directly and transact with it outside institutional intermediaries—a claim that became formalized and institutionalized through the EMD (2000) and subsequent EMI regulatory frameworks. Two sibling readings contest the same kernel: the conceptualization_reading (money emerged theoretically when David Chaum formalized digital cash cryptography, ~1985) and the infrastructure_reading (money emerged technically when electronic transfer became possible, ~1972). Each reading produces a different boundary, different beneficiaries, different victim set, and different ε. The readings do not forecclose each other—they coexist as competing frames held by different scholarly and policy communities. The consumer_holdings_reading influences both siblings by anchoring the practical instantiation that makes the competing definitions matter: without actual fintech products holding consumer money directly, the theoretical and infrastructure readings remain academic. The readings are empirically contingent: new technology (blockchain, mobile networks) or policy change (CBDC issuance, stablecoin regulation) could shift which reading's boundary becomes dominant.

omegas.question: Is 'direct consumer holdings' a stable, technically-grounded boundary for money, or is it a regulatory convenience that will fragment as technology diverges from traditional e-money instruments?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Observation of how regulatory frameworks adapt to stablecoins, CBDCs, and tokenized assets. If frameworks maintain the 'direct holdings' boundary as new instruments emerge, the boundary is robust; if the frameworks proliferate new subcategories or abandon the distinction, the boundary is contingent on regulatory choice rather than technical property.
omegas.impact: If the boundary is fragile, the entire constraint's legitimacy rests on regulatory choice rather than natural structure—reclassifying from tangled_rope toward snare (extraction sustained by regulatory enforcement rather than coordination function). If robust, the tangled_rope classification holds.
omegas.description: Whether the consumer-holdings boundary is technically robust or regulatory contingent.

omegas.question: Do fintech issuers genuinely benefit from the consumer-holdings boundary, or are they captured by regulatory requirements that make them effectively constrained?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Analysis of fintech exit options: can they pivot away from EMI licensing to other service models without losing market access? Can they move jurisdictions if regulatory burden rises? Do fintech founders report authentic optionality or constraint when asked about alternatives.
omegas.impact: If fintech are genuinely mobile beneficiaries, the constraint is tangled_rope (coordination + asymmetric extraction of banks/networks to fintech benefit). If fintech are regulatory captives, the constraint may be snare (extraction mechanisms enforced on both banks and fintech, with regulatory bodies as true beneficiaries).
omegas.description: Whether fintech issuers hold genuine beneficiary status or regulatory capture.

omegas.question: If one sibling reading (infrastructure or conceptualization) were to become dominant policy, would it logically foreclose the consumer-holdings reading, or could both coexist?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Thought experiment: a central bank defines digital money by infrastructure capability (any electronic transfer of value, regardless of custody model). Can the consumer-holdings boundary coexist with this definition, or does it logically contradict? Same test for the conceptualization reading.
omegas.impact: If siblings foreclose each other, one of the reading_relations should be 'forecloses' rather than 'coexists_with'. If coexistence is possible (different parties holding different readings), the 'coexists_with' classification holds and no mandatrophy reconciliation is forced.
omegas.description: Whether the three readings of the kernel logically exclude each other or can coexist as competing frames.

omegas.question: Is the exclusion of unbanked populations from the consumer-holdings constraint a technical inevitability (they lack device/connectivity) or a structural result of the reading's normative framing (it assumes agency/regulatory protection they don't have)?
omegas.resolution_mechanism: Comparison of fintech adoption in low-connectivity regions to theoretical penetration if infrastructure were available. If adoption remains low despite infrastructure improvement, the exclusion is normative (the reading's framing doesn't fit the population). If adoption rises with infrastructure, the exclusion is technical (not structural to the reading).
omegas.impact: If structural (normative), the constraint's beneficiary structure is narrower than claimed: the coordinate-on-direct-holdings function only works for populations with regulatory legitimacy and device access, leaving unbanked populations as permanent outsiders. This narrows the coordination benefit and raises the extraction reading.
omegas.description: Whether the unbanked exclusion is technical or structural to the reading.

network.dual_formulation_note: The digital_money_emergence_boundary kernel decomposes into three structurally distinct readings: this constraint (consumer_holdings_reading) focuses on direct consumer custody as the boundary marker and produces high extractiveness (0.62) due to fintech capture of banking revenue; the conceptualization_reading focuses on theoretical formalization (~1985) and produces lower extractiveness (estimated 0.25-0.35) because the boundary sits in the epistemic domain, not the regulatory domain; the infrastructure_reading focuses on electronic transfer capability (~1972) and produces moderate extractiveness (estimated 0.40-0.55) because it enables bypass of traditional payment networks without establishing direct consumer holdings as a necessary condition. The three readings are empirically contingent and policy-consequential: which boundary is adopted determines which fintech models are legitimate, which incumbent intermediaries lose revenue, and what central banks must measure as money supply. The readings coexist as competing frames held by different policy communities rather than foreclosing each other; the consumer_holdings_reading influences both siblings by providing the practical instantiation that makes the competing definitions economically relevant. Each reading has its own ε, beneficiary/victim set, and classification path. They are linked through network.affects_constraints to enable contamination and family analysis.
